speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In February this year, I made a Ministerial Statement on the death of Corporal First Class (CFC) National Service (NS) Aloysius Pang which had occurred on 23 January 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Therein, I gave as much detail as was known then about the incident without prejudicing the due process as prescribed by the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) Act for an independent Committee of Inquiry (COI) to investigate thoroughly the factors leading to the death.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI comprised five persons, none of whom is employed by the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) or the SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They were a judge nominated by the State Courts as Chairman; a consultant medical specialist; a member nominated by the External Review Panel on SAF Safety (ERPSS); a member drawn from the Workplace Safety and Health Council; and a senior-ranked NSman.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I remind Members that the COIs are convened under the SAF Act empowering it to fact find.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI has no mandate to determine the culpability of individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Indeed, section 8C of the SAF Act specifies that no statements made to the COI shall be admissible as evidence in the Court martial or for any subsequent disciplinary proceedings that may take place.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: To keep within this remit, I will not provide specific names of other individuals involved in the incident in my Statement, apart from CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Prosecution of any persons will be conducted separately, which I will elaborate later.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I intend to quote from their report predominantly and the dates and times stated in the report are in New Zealand local time. "On 5 January 2019, CFC(NS) Pang left Singapore for Exercise Thunder Warrior at Waiouru Military Training Area, New Zealand, as part of his seventh In-Camp Training (ICT) and the unit's eighth ICT.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Exercise Thunder Warrior is a live firing exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I draw Members' attention to the slide which I made in the Ministerial Statement in February.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you look at the picture on the top left-hand corner, the flick rammer is in the middle of the picture, the slew ring above it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And when the gun is lowered and the flick rammer goes up, he was caught between the slick rammer and the slew ring. "CFC(NS) Pang was attended to by the Battery Medic on site and evacuated to the Battalion Casualty Station (BCS) at 1910 hours.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: He was assessed and stabilised at the BCS before being evacuated to the Waiouru Base Medical Centre at 1950 hours.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At 2150 hours, CFC(NS) Pang was heli-evacuated to Waikato Hospital where he was operated on at around 0100 hours.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: CFC(NS) Pang underwent two more surgeries on 21 January and 22 January before his condition deteriorated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On 24 January 2019, CFC(NS) Pang succumbed to his injuries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: To recap from my Statement in February – the configuration, the safe positions and location of key features within the SSPH gun accompany the summary of events which we will distribute now, with your permission, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The bearing of the gun was beyond the allowable error and needed to be rectified to resume live firing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Pang was an Armament Technician from the Forward Maintenance Platoon designated to perform such work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But as CFC(NS) Pang could not resolve the issue, a Regular Military Expert 2 Technician was despatched to join him to perform the maintenance work on the gun.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I draw Members' attention that there were only three persons in the gun when the injury occurred – CFC(NS) Pang, the 3SG(NS) Gun Commander (GC) and the Regular ME2 technician (ME-Tech).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GC explained the fault to the ME-Tech.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To rectify the fault, the plan was to change the Central Processing Unit (CPU) card on the Motor Drive Control Unit – Ammo Handling System (AHS) box.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The box was located near Safe Position 3.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you remember the previous slide that was shown, the flick rammer is in the bottom left-hand corner and the box is, as indicated, near Safe Position 3.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME-Tech briefed the GC to turn off the AHS, to lock the gun barrel, turn off the engine and turn off the master switch.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To lock the gun barrel required it to be first lowered to the near-horizontal "standby" position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME-Tech then proceeded to stand at the designated Safe Position 3 and started to loosen the screws in the AHS box to carry out maintenance work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME-Tech also saw CFC(NS) Pang removing the screws on the right side of the box.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Pang was not in a designated safe position and his back was to the barrel of the gun.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Pang replied in Mandarin that it was fine and that the gun barrel would not hit him.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Before he moved the gun barrel to a standby position, the GC said he checked if the path was clear and did see CFC(NS) Pang standing near the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As the gun barrel was in the highest elevated position, the GC wrongly assumed that CFC(NS) Pang would have time to move away given that it would take some time for the barrel to move into the standby position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GC proceeded to shout, "Standby, clear away" before activating the control to move the gun.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was heard by the ME-Tech, as well as personnel who were standing outside the gun.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As the flick rammer was moving up, CFC(NS) Pang was still removing the screws on the box and looking back at the barrel at the same time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He initially made no attempt to move away.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GC noticed that CFC(NS) Pang was making some evasive movements as the barrel was moving closer to him.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME-Tech was shocked to see CFC(NS) Pang still in the path of the gun and tried to use his hands to push against the barrel to stop the movement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME-Tech tried to push the gun barrel with his hands while the GC went to the main control screen to try to stop the barrel movement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As a result, CFC(NS) Pang was wedged between the flick rammer and the slew ring.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These were the detailed events as determined by the COI that led to the serious injuries and untimely death of CFC Pang.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (b) CFC(NS) Pang did not move to a safe position, despite receiving warning that the gun barrel was going to be moved to a standby position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (c) The ME-Tech did not ensure that CFC(NS) Pang moved to a safe position, despite knowing that the gun barrel would be moved.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (d) The GC proceeded to move the gun barrel, despite noticing that CFC(NS) Pang was not in a safe position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (e) Both the GC and the ME-Tech failed to press the E-stop buttons to halt the movement of the gun barrel."  The COI determined that there was non-compliance with the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and safety breaches. "These breaches have contributed to the cause of the incident and are preventable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (a) Non-enforcement of the Safe Positions in the SSPH.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Gun Detachment Commander, ME-Tech and CFC(NS) Pang did not follow the strict requirement that everyone must be in the safe positions during the movement of the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Safe Positions 1, 2 and 3 in Members' handout.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME-Tech was standing slightly away from the Ammo Loader's position, which is Safe Position 3, and CFC(NS) Pang was standing in the path of the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Although the GC had shouted, "Standby, clear away" and the ME-Tech had told CFC(NS) Pang to move closer to him or to move away from the path of the gun barrel, both the GC and the ME-Tech did not ensure that CFC(NS) Pang was at a safe position before the gun barrel was lowered.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GC also did not adhere strictly to the SOP for lowering the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Although the GC had shouted, "Standby, clear away" before lowering the gun barrel, he should have waited for CFC(NS) Pang to be in a safe position before moving the gun barrel to the standby position but this was not adhered to.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This requirement is provided in the SSPH Operator's Manual, "that no person should be in the travel path of the barrel or the rammer tray".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GC and the ME-Tech also did not activate the E-stop buttons when the barrel was being lowered.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (b) Non-compliance with the Maintenance Manual for the SSPH Technicians.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is clearly stated in the Maintenance Manual for SSPH Technicians to ensure that before they embark on the maintenance work to replace the interface card in the AHS in this case, that the gun must be in a parked position with the gun barrel locked.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On the day of the incident, the ME-Tech did not ensure that the gun barrel was in a locked position before replacing the interface card.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Instead, the ME-Tech had started to dismantle the mountings on the gun even though the gun barrel was not in a standby or locked position." The COI opined that a combination of the following factors contributed to the cause of the incident: "(a) Lack of coordinated safety control procedure between the gun crew and the maintenance crew during maintenance work on the SSPH.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There was a lack of clarity on who should be in the gun, the command and control and whether there was a need for acknowledgement before the gun barrel is moved.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is the COI's opinion that the gun commander should take command and control to supervise and execute all preventive maintenance and corrective maintenance tasks, as well as ensure safety in the gun, as stated in the SSPH Operator's Manual.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, this does not absolve the person activating the gun barrel movement of his responsibility to ensure that everyone is in a safe position before moving the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (b) Commencing maintenance work before the gun barrel was in a locked position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME-Tech had commenced removing the mountings on the AHS box even before the gun barrel was in a locked position to get on with the job quickly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (c) Misjudgement of time and space by personnel in the SSPH.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Both the ME-Tech and the GC had miscalculated the time it took for the flick rammer to hit CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (d) Emergency Stop buttons were not activated to stop the movement of the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI found that the incident was due to the lapses of all the servicemen who were in the gun at the time of the incident – the GC, the ME-Tech and CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI also commented on factors related to but non-contributory to the incident or outcome.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Before Exercise Thunder Warrior, the SSPH guns were certified Fit for Firing (FFF) in Singapore by the technicians.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The guns were certified FFF again in New Zealand before the live firing exercise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It has been established that there was no mechanical fault with the gun that had directly caused the accident.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The incident in this case was not due to the serviceability of the SSPH.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, the COI is also of the opinion that this did not cause or contribute to the demise of CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was not for lack of knowledge of these rules or inexperience of personnel working on the SSPH gun.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI determined that prior to the incident, all the three personnel in the gun – CFC(NS) Pang, the GC and the ME-Tech – had received adequate training to be aware that whenever the gun barrel is moved, they must be in a safe position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was clear to the ME-Tech that CFC(NS) Pang was not in a safe position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Notwithstanding this, the ME-Tech merely told CFC(NS) Pang to move closer to him or move away, instead of stopping the gun movement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When CFC(NS) Pang replied that the gun barrel would not hit him and did not move away from where he was, the ME-Tech could have ensured that CFC(NS) Pang moved away to a safe position or pressed the E-stop button.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GC shouted, "Standby, clear away" before he commenced lowering the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the same time, he saw that CFC(NS) Pang was not standing in a designated safe position.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Instead of ensuring that CFC(NS) Pang was in a safe position before lowering the gun barrel, he thought that there was sufficient time for CFC(NS) Pang to move away as the gun barrel was lowered.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From the accounts of CFC(NS) Pang's peers to the COI, CFC(NS) Pang had a positive work attitude and was very helpful to others when it came to work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He was also professional when executing his tasks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Pang started his Full-time National Service in October 2008.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He had attended several courses and training during his Full-Time National Service, graduating with an overall "A" grade from the Armament Basic Technician Training (Turret).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He had also attended the Maintenance Vocational Training on his sixth ICT in February 2018 in preparation for Exercise Thunder Warrior.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He was also professional when executing his tasks and was seen by his superiors as someone who would not cut safety corners when working." Nevertheless, the COI found that the incident was due to lapses of all the servicemen who were in the gun at the time of the incident.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Army safety culture should be enhanced and special emphasis should also be placed on the safety culture of the NSmen who must be equally cognisant of all safety regulations and procedures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF could involve NS commanders in the review of the Training Safety Regulations (TSRs) as this will instil greater ownership by NSmen in terms of safety.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF should review all SOPs and drills to ensure that there are proper procedures in mixed-crew operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SOP for maintenance work involving gun crew and maintenance crew should be established, including hand-over procedures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Emergency drills or SOPs should be developed to educate operators on the application of E-Stop buttons during gun barrel movements.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (c) Ensure compliance to TSRs, SOPs and Operator Manuals.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All systems should be operated in the manner required by their design and a new risk assessment should be conducted if any part of the system is to be used differently.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is also a need to ensure that SOPs relating to the operations of the gun are complied with and operations should be halted whenever the SOPs are not complied with.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similarly, there must be strict enforcement that the equipment conditions as mandated in the maintenance manual is adhered to before the commencement of maintenance work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (d) Enhance existing training/safety support, especially for maintenance-related work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A safety checklist briefing before the start of any maintenance works could be introduced, with emphasis on the number of maintenance crew needed to work inside the gun.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (e) Enhance training of Medical Officers for aero-medical evacuation and pre-hospital care.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Given the extended distances to definitive care – one of the principal considerations in the Medical Support Plan – the use of helicopters for casualty evacuation to a higher echelon care is a given.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A familiarisation of the RSAF heli-evacuation protocols should be considered for both NSF and NSmen Medical Officers posted to this specific area of training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: NSmen Medical Officers could also re-familiarise themselves with acute trauma care by being given temporary registration as observers either in the emergency and surgery departments during call-ups.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (f) Improve protocols for communications within hospitals caring for injured Servicemen overseas.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It may be useful to formalise arrangements between the SAF and receiving hospitals at the appropriate level in the hospital administration so that our Singaporean doctors attached to care for the injured servicemen overseas can be kept abreast of clinical developments and can contribute more effectively.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (g) Lastly, formalise protocols for overseas hospitals following death of SAF personnel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ERPSS also expressed concern about the safety lapses and weaknesses in safety culture that have been surfaced and made several recommendations that would help the SAF to build a stronger safety culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, it is important for commanders to exercise leadership in safety and impress upon their subordinates the need to properly implement safety policies and procedures, build a strong safety culture, and inculcate stronger safety ownership at both team and individual levels, especially among NSmen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, the SAF should do more to improve knowledge retention and safety awareness in its soldiers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Third, it is vital to accord the same high level of emphasis on maintenance safety, as is accorded to training safety today.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Last, it is crucial to strengthen safety procedures for mixed-crew operations, which can be potentially risky if differences in practices across vocations are not properly addressed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Specifically, the IGO has identified the need for the SAF to improve in three key areas: command emphasis on safety, safety as a mission outcome and team safety culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF has to ensure that there is internalisation of safety as a mission outcome across all levels of command.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All commanders must adopt a zero-accident mindset and set it in the heart of their unit safety culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When coupled with a healthy open reporting culture, we can prevent the next accident from happening as our units share with others lessons learnt from safety incidents and near misses.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Another key element of a strong safety culture is team safety.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our commanders need to build a strong culture of team safety, where soldiers take responsibility for their own safety, look out for their buddies and keep one another safe during all training and mixed-crew activities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These behaviours must be ingrained into every soldier, sailor and airman so that safety rules are observed at all times.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Following this incident, the SAF has also taken specific steps to strengthen personal ownership of safety and enhance safety for maintenance-related training or tasks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (a) Specifically, a Think-Check-Do drill will be implemented as a routine part of pre-maintenance task checks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As part of the drill, technicians will plan and brief all personnel of their expected roles and tasks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A dry run of team-based maintenance tasks will be conducted to ensure tight integration.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The positions of E-stop buttons will be re-emphasised together with E-stop procedures and rehearsed as part of pre-ops drills.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (b) Safe areas and hazardous areas will be further emphasised through bold markings on platforms as part of safety enhancements.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (c) The SAF will entrench safety ownership at the team level so that it will become ingrained for soldiers to take care of themselves, their servicemen and their buddies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Safety advocates will be appointed in the units to emphasise safety and conduct checks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (e) NSmen will be actively involved in safety reviews where they can give feedback on safety matters before, during and after each training activity, and this feedback will be incorporated into our TSR reviews.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: (f) Medical Officers will be required to undergo refresher training on heli-evacuation processes prior to their deployment for overseas medical support.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: New initiatives will also be explored to enhance their exposure to acute trauma care.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We need a strong SAF that can defend Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it must and can be built up without compromising the safety and well-being of our NSmen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF is committed to continue strengthening its safety systems at all levels, down to our soldiers, aircrew and sailors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I want to put on record our appreciation to the COI members who have put in much effort and time to thoroughly investigate this tragic incident.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And, in that process, they interviewed more than 20 persons involved with the incident, and reviewed voluminous documents related to the event and manuals related to instructions and safety procedures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Pang's death occurred in New Zealand, which therefore has state jurisdiction and not our Police or State Coroner.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, the New Zealand Attorney-General exercised his discretion not to undertake any inquiry for CFC(NS) Pang's case.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Under our military law, it therefore falls on the SAF's Special Investigation Branch (SIB) with the jurisdiction to investigate CFC(NS) Pang's death.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They will decide if any servicemen are to be prosecuted in a military Court for offences related to CFC(NS) Pang's death.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The military Court is presided over by former or serving State Court judges as Presidents of the General Court Martial (GCM).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GCM will have full access to the witnesses to independently make their own findings and conclusions on the culpability of the individuals who may be charged.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The GCM need not take into account anything in my Statement in Parliament today.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the meantime, servicemen under investigation are reassigned to administrative duties and, if found to have been culpable, will be charged and punished accordingly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We know that it is a difficult time for them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Pang was by all accounts a motivated and competent soldier.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He was well-liked; he was trusted by his peers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The loss of a good soldier like CFC(NS) Pang is deeply grievous to us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There was an outpouring of grief from many Singaporeans as a result of his untimely and tragic demise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It pertains to the first handout, the summary of COI's findings on the chronology of events, specifically item (6) where the ME-Tech informed CFC(NS) Pang in a mixture of Mandarin and English that the gun barrel was going to be moved to the "standby" position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And thereafter, the late CFC(NS) Pang replied in Mandarin that it was fine and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first question really pertains to the communication among the servicemen in the turret, whether the COI found a language to be an issue amongst the servicemen, whether the reaction time was slowed because of these issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Looking forward, and I think for servicemen who are born in Singapore, we probably understand a little bit of Mandarin and Malay, if you are an Indian.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But for certain servicemen who could be new citizens, language could be an issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, how does SAF intend to resolve issues that could crop up where in a situation of extreme panic, language potentially could be a cause for an accident?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will neither impute or raise new items because we want to keep within the remit of the COI.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was quite clear to all three in the gun of the safety procedures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said, the COI made explicit reference that they knew the safety rules, ex ante, before they went to do maintenance and while they were doing maintenance; and while the gun barrel was moved.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All three were clear that no one should stand in the path of the gun barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And there was no indication that CFC(NS) Pang did not understand or took a longer time to understand that the gun barrel was moving into him and he was still in the path.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And it is, indeed, a very sad incident.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In any situation where people are trusted to do things, there is a risk of human error.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I notice that the Committee's recommendations are largely all incremental in nature, including the emphasis on personal responsibility for safety, reviewing the SOPs and ensuring compliance in the SOPs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But then again, all these things have to be delegated to people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, is there anything we can really do as a system to try and deal with this risk of leaving people to do things?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I spent a few years as Minister for Manpower.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I set up the Workplace Safety Council during my tenure as Minister and visited a number of safety systems.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was following, if Members remember, the two incidents at Fusionpolis and Nicoll Highway.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For these two incidents, we undertook a safety review, as Mr Vikram Nair has said, of the systems, we went to visit a number of other countries which have better safety records.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Professionally, all the safety officers or those who have been involved with these, will tell you it boils down to culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is just not the articulation of rules.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is how you internalise every act to the point that you take that extra effort.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can tell people that you have to put on seat belts; you can tell people you should not use your handphone while you are driving.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is no rule that says that you should not look at your handphone while crossing the road.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, for us, we do not have that luxury to just tell people.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are an organisation; we are responsible for NSmen that are sent to us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And you have to do it in a systematic way to tighten, first of all, is it lack of knowledge or is it unclear rules or rules that are difficult to follow?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If we find any of these, then you amend them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But ultimately, where we have reached is that you have to take care of yourself and your buddy; and you have to internalise this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we found, in fact, a gap, that while we are paying a lot of attention to live firing exercises, one would think that, in maintenance, you do not have high risk.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And yet, here, you have an incident where you ignored the safety rules and something very tragic happens.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, you have to inculcate that, "Accidents do not take holidays".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You have to be very careful about the rules.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The rules there are written for a reason.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, did any personnel involved ever declare that there might be operational reasons to not follow aspects of the SOP?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They could not wait for that few seconds, and for whatever reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Did they interview others to see the situation on the ground?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is what the SAF, the Army, the Artillery and the IGO asked themselves.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you have an isolated incident here and there, you can fix it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And this is my surmising – this is nothing to do with the COI; the COI did not say this – I think NSmen or crew operators can understand when the gun is being fired and at great speeds, and if it hits you, serious injuries, so you better pay attention to the rules.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But you underestimate, even at maintenance, that how can this happen?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, that just drives home the point that you have to observe safety rules that rigorously.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We must not make safety rules so onerous that you cannot comply.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That, indeed, is the thinking, and I thank the Member for that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is equivalent to house-proofing when a new baby arrives.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But the big difference is, remember that our equipment must function in war or in battle.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you build enough automatic stop systems, when we have to push the button and go, we have to push many buttons to start deactivating things that we have put into place.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Can you do it for the training equipment?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And you would remember that when we spoke about the Bionix incident, that, indeed, is what we have done.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have got buttons that somebody can stop.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we have only done it for training equipment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We know the cost of the SAF, not only in terms of resources and in money, but in persons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We take it seriously and we will design our systems to design away flaws as much as we can, always with the eye that it must not render us operationally incapable or put us at a disadvantage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, I have one clarification for the Minister for Defence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in his speech, he mentioned that the New Zealand Attorney-General (AG) exercised his discretion and declined to investigate the incident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, we know from other instances, for example, Gavin Chan's death in Australia, that the Queensland authorities did actually investigate and there was a Coroner's Inquiry held there.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister: did the New Zealand AG indicate any reason why he declined to do so?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, should such an unfortunate incident happen in other countries, would we or would we not expect the foreign government to investigate?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Be mindful that we are training in some other country and we are subject to their jurisdiction and we have to respect their laws.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In Australia's situation, I am not sure that he had the discretion to not investigate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, in this case, the AG decided that they would not and, therefore, we started the COI.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That was not to mean that even if they did investigate, we will not have a COI.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it was now, in the Australian case, as the Member said, Gavin Chan's case, there were two sets of investigations – theirs and our COI.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI did not give any mention that time pressure was in any way contributory to the injury or death.
